newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Palm sees no inflation threat from weak mark.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Palm sees no inflation threat from weak mark.

text.p: A senior Bundesbanker on Friday played down the possible impact of the recent weakening of the mark, saying he did not expect it to fuel domestic inflation.

Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm told Reuters in an interview that while the dollar at its present level of between 1.79 or 1.80 marks would lift import prices, its impact on consumer inflation would be curbed by high unemployment.

A further significant dollar rise would have to be closely monitored but the dollar exchange rate on its own did not determine the Bundesbank's monetary policy, said Palm, who is president of the state central bank of Baden-Wuerttemberg.
Asked whether he saw a danger that a sustained dollar rate of 1.79 marks or 1.80 marks could increase inflationary pressures in Germany in the foreseeable future, Palm said:
"The depreciation of a currency in itself always has an impact on import prices.

"But given that the economy is by no means foaming over, given continued labour market problems and the far-reaching consequences of companies boosting productivity and cutting costs, I see no appreciable deterioration of the domestic price climate at present."
Palm's comments came at the end of week which has seen policymakers take a relatively sanguine view of the mark's steep weakening on foreign exchanges.
That is partly because the mark's decline has bestowed sharp earnings increases on the country's giant export sector, thereby helping drive share prices to record highs.

Several Bundesbank officials have said they see no reason to raise interest rates to stem the mark's fall, and Chancellor Helmut Kohl, speaking earlier on Friday at a news conference in Bonn, said the recent strength of the U.S. dollar against the mark was "not earth-shaking."

"When exports used to go badly because of a weak dollar, people complained," Kohl told a news conference. "Now things are going a bit the other way, which is not earth-shaking, it does not mean that we should start moving."

Palm stressed that the Bundesbank's monetary policy was guided by how the money supply developed and noted that M3 money supply growth was close to the Bundesbank's target growth of 3.5 to 6.5 percent for 1997.
M3 for June is expected to be released early next week and analysts predict annualised M3 growth for the month slowed to 6.8 percent or 6.9 percent from 7.0 percent in May.
Palm also said he saw no reason now to depart from its system of fixing its main money market rate, or repo rate, itself, rather than allowing banks a say in setting the rate.

The comment quelled market speculation that the Bundesbank may revert to so-called variable-rate weekly tenders for its securities repurchase agreements, or repos, in a move which may nudge the repo rate higher and thereby give markets a signal
